input:
# Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) Deep Dive

Background: HPA was introduced in Kubernetes 1.2 to automatically scale workloads based on observed CPU utilization or custom metrics.

How it works: The HPA controller queries the metrics API every 15 seconds (configurable via --horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period). It computes the desired replica count using: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas * (currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue)).

Known issues:
- Scale-down is intentionally delayed (default 5 minutes) to prevent thrashing.
- Custom metrics require the custom.metrics.k8s.io API to be registered.

Action items:
- Tune --horizontal-pod-autoscaler-downscale-stabilization for your workload.
- Enable KEDA for event-driven autoscaling when HPA is insufficient.

References:
https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/
https://keda.sh

input:
# Distributed Tracing with OpenTelemetry

Background: Distributed tracing emerged as a necessity when monolithic applications were decomposed into microservices. Each user request now traverses dozens of services, making it impossible to debug latency issues without end-to-end visibility.

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is a CNCF project that provides a unified observability framework. It consolidates the previously fragmented landscape of tracing libraries (Jaeger client, Zipkin client, OpenCensus) into a single vendor-neutral SDK.

Core concepts:
- Trace: a DAG of Spans representing a complete request lifecycle
- Span: a single unit of work with start/end timestamps, attributes, and events
- Context propagation: passing trace context across process boundaries via W3C TraceContext headers (traceparent, tracestate)
- Exporter: sends telemetry data to a backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, Datadog)

Sampling strategies:
- Always-on: 100% of traces captured (high cost in production)
- Head-based: sampling decision at trace root
- Tail-based: decision after full trace is assembled (requires a collector like otelcol)

Instrumentation approaches:
1. Auto-instrumentation: agent injects bytecode (Java, Python, Node.js) — zero code changes
2. Manual instrumentation: explicit SDK calls — more control, language-agnostic

Setup example (Go):
```go
tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(
    sdktrace.WithBatcher(exporter),
    sdktrace.WithResource(res),
)
otel.SetTracerProvider(tp)
```

Known issues:
- Baggage propagation can leak sensitive data across service boundaries if not carefully scoped.
- Auto-instrumentation for Go is not yet stable (requires eBPF-based approach).

Action items:
- Adopt otelcol (OpenTelemetry Collector) as the central telemetry pipeline rather than exporting directly from services.
- Define a sampling policy: tail-based at 1% for high-traffic endpoints, 100% for errors.

References:
https://opentelemetry.io/docs/
https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go

input:
The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can only guarantee two of the following three properties simultaneously: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance.

Background: Formulated by Eric Brewer in 2000 and later proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002, CAP has guided distributed systems design for over two decades.

In practice, network partitions are unavoidable in real distributed systems, so the real trade-off is between CP (consistent, partition-tolerant) and AP (available, partition-tolerant) systems. Examples: HBase, Zookeeper (CP); Cassandra, DynamoDB (AP).

Conclusion: CAP theorem is a useful mental model but oversimplifies the design space. The PACELC model extends it by also considering latency trade-offs under normal operation.

References:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAP_theorem
https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/564585.564601
